lesson.title: Between Two Fences: Solving Absolute Value Inequalities
lesson.summary: Absolute value inequalities translate into a bounded interval for a less than symbol or two separate rays for a greater than symbol, building directly on the splitting technique used for absolute value equations.
lesson.body:
Absolute value equations split into two separate equations because a distance can point two directions. Absolute value inequalities work the same way, but now instead of two exact numbers, you get a range of numbers, because you are asking not which numbers are exactly this far away, but which numbers are closer than this or which numbers are farther than this. The direction of the inequality symbol, less than or greater than, completely changes the shape of the answer, so recognizing which case you are in is the first and most important decision in the whole problem.

When the inequality is |expression| < a, with a positive, you are looking for numbers whose distance from zero is smaller than a, which means the expression is squeezed between negative a and a. That translates into the compound inequality negative a < expression < a, one connected statement joining two inequalities. When the inequality is |expression| > a, you are looking for numbers whose distance from zero is bigger than a, which means the expression is either far to the right or far to the left, so it splits into expression > a OR expression < negative a, two separate, disconnected statements. A useful memory trick is that less than stays connected in the middle, while greater than breaks apart into two options.

Work through an example of each type. First solve |x - 4| < 6. Since this is a less than case, rewrite it as -6 < x - 4 < 6. Add 4 to all three parts: -6 + 4 < x < 6 + 4, which simplifies to -2 < x < 10. Check with a value inside the interval, like x = 0: |0 - 4| = |-4| = 4, and 4 < 6 is true. Check a value outside, like x = 11: |11 - 4| = |7| = 7, and 7 < 6 is false, confirming that 11 correctly falls outside the solution set.

Now solve |x + 2| >= 5. Since this is a greater than or equal case, split it into two separate inequalities: x + 2 >= 5, or x + 2 <= -5. Solving the first gives x >= 3. Solving the second gives x <= -7. The solution set is everything less than or equal to -7, together with everything greater than or equal to 3, two rays pointing away from each other rather than one connected interval. Testing x = 4 in the original inequality gives |4 + 2| = |6| = 6, and 6 is greater than or equal to 5, confirming that x = 4 belongs to the solution.

Just as with absolute value equations, always isolate the absolute value expression before splitting into cases, and remember that an absolute value expression set to be less than a negative number has no solution, while one set to be greater than a negative number is true for every real number, since distance is never negative. Recognizing these boundary cases quickly saves time and prevents you from chasing a solution that either does not exist or already includes everything. When you graph the solution on a number line, a less than compound inequality shades one connected segment between two endpoints, using open circles if the inequality is strict, while a greater than split shades two separate rays heading in opposite directions, a visual reminder that the two case types genuinely produce different shapes of answer, not just different symbols.
